83.t: Mafia connections and a record label owner's trouble
83.s: He was never strong-armed; mobsters' girlfriends occasionally recorded, and one label owner who took Marcello money was caught and beaten.
83.q: Now, now and then one of them would have a girlfriend or somebody wanted to sing, you know, and they'd do a session with them. I probably did a dozen sessions over the years with some nightclub owner's girlfriend, you know.

4.t: Sheffield's trial, transfer and later life as a photographer
4.s: Sheffield, rumored to be the police chief's half-brother, escaped conviction, was moved from Central Avenue, then became a photographer.
4.ch: Central Avenue clubs, Nordskog, Sheffield and Music Town

641.t: Officer Sheffield, the tough Prohibition detective
641.s: Joe describes Sheffield as a huge Black detective who raided bootleg joints but spared musicians, and the Sonny Clay record named for him.
641.ch: Los Angeles nightlife: Sheffield, Hamp and the Cotton Club
641.q: Anybody that knew anything about Prohibition remembers Sheffield. He was a tough cop, man. Sheffield would arrest his mother if she's bootlegging.

641.t: The raid where Sheffield said Every tub
641.s: Joe tells of a house-rent party where Sheffield joked Every tub, and mentions the other detectives Black Benny and Green.
641.ch: Los Angeles nightlife: Sheffield, Hamp and the Cotton Club
641.q: Any musician that lived here in Los Angeles that had two tough cops... Sheffield was a Black policeman, and they had a White policeman named Sweetman -- which was a tough character, too. They caught you in one of them joints, they'd put you in jail. But what Sheffield would do, now... They claimed…

412.s: Hodes says McGovern's welcomed fights, and compares the Brass Rail in 1957 where football players were thrown out. He also tells how a policeman was given a mickey and his gun laid on the bar.
412.q: And he was drinking real whisky. So it was a colorful place of its time. Another thing about McGovern's, they didn't mind having a fight there at all. 113.s: McShann tells of the club in Ponca City, Oklahoma where Indians, whites and blacks mixed and a bouncer called Alligator cleared the room when fights broke out.
